rules.statement: A read path that returns only an asymmetric key's public half must use the stored public key and must never unprotect, decrypt or load the private key, or acquire a secret protector or master key, to derive it.
rules.why: Deriving the public key from the stored secret loads the owner's master keys, may reach the key management service, and holds private key material in memory just to answer a read of public data.
rules.check: Look for public-key, JWKS or registration `jwks` read code that injects or calls a secret protector or unprotect method, or deserializes the private secret and then exports its public part.

rules.statement: When an asymmetric private or remote key is generated or imported, persist its public half beside it as base64url SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER, not as a JWK or PEM.
rules.why: SPKI is what every key-type descriptor already deserializes. A JWK's `kid`, `use` and `alg` can change after the key is stored, and PEM would be a second format.
rules.check: Look for new persisted public-key fields or values that store a JWK JSON string, PEM text, or a format other than SPKI DER.

rules.statement: Don't store a separate public-key copy for a secret whose own encoding is already public (SPKI or X.509), or for symmetric and verifier secrets; leave the field null and read the public key from the secret's own encoded value.
rules.why: A copy would only repeat the encoded value, an X.509 secret would lose its certificate, and symmetric secrets have no public half.
rules.check: Look for code that fills the stored public-key field for spki, x509, symmetric or verifier secrets.

rules.statement: Every update path that rebuilds a persisted secret record must copy its stored public key into the new record.
rules.why: Public-key reads depend only on the stored public half. If an update drops it, the public key can no longer be read without touching private material.
rules.check: In secret update or rebuild code that builds a new persisted record, check that the public-key property is carried over along with the other fields.

rules.statement: Produce a public JWK through the key type's registered descriptor export, the same one the JWKS endpoint uses, and never through a separate JWK serializer in another layer.
rules.why: A second serializer would drift from the descriptor in curve names and member encoding, and sharing the export means a new key type works on both surfaces.
rules.check: Look for code outside the key-type descriptors that writes JWK members (`kty`, `crv`, `n`, `e`, `x`, `y` and so on) by hand to export a public key.

rules.statement: Keep secret read and list resources metadata-only: expose a secret's public key through a separate read-only sub-resource and don't add key material fields to the shared secret resource.
rules.why: Key material on the shared read contract bloats the resource and the list with data that is only sometimes wanted, and couples the metadata view to key export.
rules.check: Look for public-key, JWK, PEM or key-material properties added to a secret metadata resource or list item type.

rules.statement: A public-key endpoint must return 404 for a secret that has no public half (a symmetric secret, a key type that exports none, or no stored public key), and must not unprotect the secret to find that out.
rules.why: 404 is the honest answer, and a symmetric secret should never be unprotected just to learn that it has no public key.
rules.check: Look at public-key endpoint handlers to see that the missing-public-key case returns 404 and is decided from metadata and the stored public key alone.

rules.statement: Authorize a read of a secret's public key the same way as a read of the secret itself, and don't add a new scope for it.
rules.why: The decision gives the public-key sub-resource the same read authorization as the secret and adds no scope.
rules.check: Look for a new scope or policy, or a different authorization requirement, on a public-key sub-resource endpoint compared with the secret read endpoint.
